dedupe_keys.name: united states nested food and economic system resilience with networked input output analysis 2007 and 2012

description: This case study treats the US food system as embedded in the whole economy and uses networked input-output analysis to study its resilience to real and simulated shocks. The authors, Catherine Brinkley of the University of California, Davis, John Ulimwengu of the International Food Policy Research Institute and Subhashni Raj of the University of Hawaii at Manoa, compared the US food and economic system in 2007 and 2012, a period spanning the financial crisis, and simulated the removal of the most central sectors. The article was published in September 2025 in Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems and is free to read online under a Creative Commons Attribution licence. Coverage is the national economy. Caveats: input-output tables are aggregate and static, and simulated removals are stylised shocks. Between 2007 and 2012, 82.2 percent of food system sectors increased in centrality relative to other sectors, showing the food system became more integral to the economy during and after the crisis. Removing the most central sectors reduced network density, clustering and degree, showing vulnerabilities that could propagate system-wide. The authors highlight scientific research as a sector needing little funding that amplifies outputs across the food system, and warn against analysing food systems outside the wider economy. Simulation uses: a sector network method for food supply cascading failure and economic shock models. Related records: the global staple trade network cascade study (case_study-global-staple-food-trade-network-resilience-cascading-failure) and the DARTS food system model (model-darts-food-system) address shock propagation at global scale.
